lessons.title: Case Study: Fading India VIX Spikes Around Results and Elections

children.text: India VIX has produced two of its most dramatic moves in recent memory around two very different kinds of events. In March 2020, as the scale of the Covid-19 shock became clear, India VIX surged to its highest level on record, above 80, before gradually normalizing back toward its long-run range of roughly 12 to 15 over the following year. On 4 June 2024, the day Lok Sabha election results were declared, India VIX had already been climbing through the preceding sessions as exit polls stoked uncertainty, spiked further as the Nifty swung sharply on the results themselves, then fell back within days once the outcome was fully known. Same instrument, same broad pattern, one resolved in days, the other took the better part of a year. This case study builds the framework for telling those two situations apart in advance.

body.text: A VIX spike eventually reverting is not the same thing as a VIX spike being a good trade today. What makes an event-driven spike tradeable is knowing, in advance, roughly when the uncertainty resolves. A spike with no such date attached might revert just as surely, but nobody entering the trade can know how long that will take, which is a very different risk to underwrite.

children.text: Two Real Episodes, Two Very Different Trades

body.caption: March 2020 vs 4 June 2024: both eventually reverted, on very different timelines

cells: A genuine, open-ended global health and economic shock
A sharp, multi-year local high, well below the 2020 record
Was the resolution date known in advance?
No. Nobody trading the spike in real time knew how the pandemic would unfold
Yes. The election result date was fixed and public weeks in advance

body.text: It is tempting to look back and say the 2020 VIX spike "reverted, so it was mean reversion working". That is true only with hindsight. A trader fading that spike in the third week of March 2020 had no way of knowing whether normalization would take three weeks or three years, or whether VIX would spike even higher first, which it did. This is exactly why Lesson 14 placed open-ended crises on the unreliable side of the table, regardless of what eventually happened. The election result, by contrast, had a fixed, known date the entire time, which is what made it a genuinely different, tighter risk to underwrite.

children.text: A systematic version of this lesson combines two checks that neither Chapter 2's statistics nor Chapter 1's fundamental judgment can provide alone: a statistical stretch (VIX's percentile rank, from Lesson 14) and a calendar check (is there a specific, dated, scheduled catalyst that plausibly explains the spike, within a defined lookahead window). A spike clearing both bars is treated as a higher-confidence candidate. A spike clearing only the statistical bar, with no identifiable scheduled catalyst, gets flagged for closer fundamental review before being treated as tradeable, exactly the same discipline Chapter 1 applied to individual stocks, now applied to volatility itself.

Take a hypothetical illustration built around a Union Budget date, five trading sessions away. India VIX has been climbing as the market waits, and the screen tracks both its level and its trailing one-year percentile rank each day.

body.caption: A hypothetical VIX screen through a Budget event window

body.title: Hypothetical India VIX path through a scheduled Budget event

body.label: What clears the screen
body.context: By the day before the event, VIX has cleared a high statistical bar (88th percentile) and there is a specific, dated, known catalyst five sessions away. Both conditions from the systematic screen are satisfied.

children.text: Translating this VIX path into an actual rupee profit and loss for an options position requires option pricing mechanics, strike selection, and time decay, deliberately outside this course's scope. What this lesson gives you is the screen itself: a statistically stretched reading, paired with a known, dated resolution point, is what turns "VIX looks high" into a structured hypothesis worth investigating further with the appropriate options tools and your broker.

body.text: Contrast the Budget scenario with a VIX reading that also clears the 90th percentile but with no scheduled catalyst on the calendar, no results season, no policy date, no election, just a drift higher on diffuse, general nervousness. That is the harder case. It might still be a good fade. It might also be the early stage of a genuine, unscheduled deterioration, the volatility-domain equivalent of Yes Bank's early warning signs in Chapter 1, before anyone could put a date on how it would resolve. The percentile rank alone cannot tell these two situations apart. The calendar check is what does the real work.

body.title: Compute today's VIX percentile rank
body.prompt: Over the trailing 10 sessions (not including today), India VIX closed at: 11, 12, 19, 13, 14, 21, 12, 15, 13, 16. Today it closes at 17. Using Lesson 14's definition, percentile rank equals the percentage of the trailing window's sessions with a lower value than today, what is today's percentile rank?
body.explanation: Eight of the ten trailing values (11, 12, 13, 14, 12, 15, 13, 16) are below 17. Only two (19 and 21) are above it. 8 out of 10 is an 80th percentile rank, a statistically stretched, though not extreme, reading.

body.title: Which spike fits the systematic screen?
body.question: Two stocks' worth of context, applied to India VIX. Scenario A: VIX is at the 91st percentile, with a scheduled RBI policy announcement four trading sessions away. Scenario B: VIX is also at the 91st percentile, drifting up gradually over three weeks with no identifiable scheduled catalyst on the calendar. Which scenario better fits this lesson's systematic screen for a higher-confidence volatility reversion candidate?
options: Scenario A, because it clears both the statistical bar and the calendar check
Scenario B, because a slower, gradual rise is always more predictable than a sharp one
Both are equally strong candidates since the percentile rank is identical
Neither qualifies, since India VIX itself cannot be traded directly
body.explanation: Scenario A clears both conditions in the systematic screen: a high percentile rank and a specific, dated, known catalyst within a short lookahead window. Scenario B matches only the statistical bar, with no calendar-based explanation, which Lesson 14's table flags as the less reliable, open-ended-style case, even at an identical percentile rank.

points: A VIX spike eventually reverting, as the March 2020 spike eventually did, is not the same as it being a good trade at the time. Reliability depends on whether the resolution date was knowable in advance, not on whether reversion happened eventually.

The 4 June 2024 election results episode and the March 2020 Covid-19 crash both saw India VIX spike and later normalize, on completely different timelines, precisely because one had a known, dated resolution and the other did not.

A systematic screen for volatility reversion combines a statistical stretch check (percentile rank) with a calendar check (a specific, dated, scheduled catalyst within a defined window), mirroring Chapter 1's fundamental discipline applied to volatility.
A high percentile rank with no identifiable scheduled catalyst is a harder, less reliable case, it may still revert, but it could equally be the early stage of a genuine, unscheduled deterioration.

This closes Chapter 4. Chapter 5 moves from volatility back to price, but at a slower, valuation-level pace: whether stretched P/E multiples and out-of-favor sectors revert the same way individual price deviations do.
